**GitHub repo:** <https://github.com/enzocast1/ec422_ps3_Castaldo>

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(seasonal)
```

## Time and Tsibbles

**The two datasets.** `retail_ts` holds U.S. retail and food services sales from the Census Bureau's monthly retail trade survey, downloaded from FRED, in millions of dollars. It contains two series stacked in long format: `RSAFS` (seasonally adjusted) and `RSAFSNA` (not seasonally adjusted). It is monthly, its index is `Month` (a `yearmonth`), and its key is `series_id`. `can_gas` is monthly natural gas production in Canada, in billions of cubic meters, from January 1960 to February 2005, taken from the `canadian_gas` tsibble in the `fpp3` package. Its index is `Month`, and it has no key because it holds only one series.

### 2.2 Reading the data

```{r}
retail_raw <- read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv")
head(retail_raw)
```

**2.2a.** The `observation_date` column is read in as `<date>`, so `read_csv()` guessed the type correctly.

```{r}
retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/retail_sales_raw.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    RSAFS = col_double(),
    RSAFSNA = col_double()
  )
)
```

### 2.3 Long format

```{r}
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")

head(retail_raw_long)
```

### 2.4 Building the tsibble

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)

head(retail_ts)
has_gaps(retail_ts)
```

**2.4b.** The header shows `[1M]`, so the tsibble correctly detected a monthly frequency, and `has_gaps()` returns `FALSE` for both series, so there are no gaps in the monthly dates.

### 2.5 Canadian gas production

```{r}
key_vars(canadian_gas)
index_var(canadian_gas)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume)

has_gaps(can_gas)
head(can_gas)
```

### 2.6 Working with dates

```{r}
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))

can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(year    = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))

can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume))
```

**2.6b.** \[FILL IN from the table above: the month with the highest average production is Jan and the month with the lowest is Jun

```{r}
can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
```

```{r}
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))

head(can_gas_q)

can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume)
```

**2.6d.** We sum the monthly values rather than taking their mean because gas production is based on flow: each month's value is the volume produced that month, so adding the three months gives the total volume produced in the quarter. The quarterly series is still seasonal, it shows a repeating in thhe year pattern, and the size of the seasonal swings changes over time.

### 2.7 Plotting

```{r}
retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)
```

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.7b.** Seasonal adjustment removes the seasonal component from the data, which lets us see the trend more clearly. The NSA series has a repeating pattern every year, sales spike in December and drop sharply in January, while the SA series is smooth and has no such pattern. Both series follow the same long-run path, rising over time and dropping during the 2008 recession and the 2020 COVID shutdown, so seasonal adjustment does not change the overall trend or the recessions. The NSA seasonal swings also get larger over time as the level of sales grows.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Monthly, not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Billions of cubic meters"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.7d.** I added `scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)` to replace the scientific-notation axis labels (like 2e+05) with comma-formatted numbers, which makes the sales values easier to read.

## Transformations

### 3.1 Logs

**3.1a.** The seasonal swings in `can_gas` grow as the series grows in the early years, but this is not true over the whole sample: the swings are largest from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s and then shrink from around 1990 onward, even though production keeps rising.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Monthly, not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Log(billions of cubic meters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1b.** After taking logs, the seasonal swings are still uneven: largest in the 1970s-80s and smallest after the mid-1990s,so logging does not make the seasonal swings the same size. The trend grows steeply in the 1960s, flattens out around the mid-1970s, rises again in the late 1980s-1990s, and levels off around 2000. I don't think logs are necessary for `can_gas`, because logs work best when the seasonal swings grow in proportion to the level of the series, and here the swings shrink in the later years even as production keeps rising.

```{r}
retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail Sales (NSA)",
    subtitle = "Level",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail Sales (NSA)",
    subtitle = "Log",
    x = NULL, y = "Log(millions of dollars)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1c.** The case for logging is stronger than it was for `can_gas`. In levels, the seasonal swings in retail sales grow as sales grow, and after taking logs the swings at the start of the sample are roughly the same size as at the end, which means the swings grew in proportion to the level of the series. This wasn't true for `can_gas`, where the swings grew and then shrank.

### 3.2 Growth rates

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct  = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth in Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Month-over-month percent change (direct)",
    x = NULL, y = "Percent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Gap Between Direct and Log-Difference Growth Rates",
    subtitle = "Canadian natural gas production",
    x = NULL, y = "Absolute difference (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.2b.** The log difference is a good approximation in most months, with gaps mostly under 0.5 percentage points, but it becomes less accurate in months with very large growth rates, especially in the early 1960s, when the gap reaches about 3 percentage points.

### 3.3 SA vs. NSA growth rates

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.3.** The SA series month-over-month growth rates hover around 0 percent, apart from large moves during the 2020 COVID shutdown and rebound. The NSA series is much noisier, with growth rates swinging from about -30 to almost 30 percent. This is because the NSA series is not seasonally adjusted: those swings come from its seasonal component. This connects back to 2.7b, where the NSA level spiked every December and dropped every January; in growth rates, that pattern shows up as a large positive growth rate in December and a large negative one in January every year. The SA series has had the seasonal component removed, so its growth rates are much smoother and more stable.

## Seasonality

### 4.1 Season plots

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1b.** In the NSA season plot, every year's line traces the same shape: sales are low in January and February and spike in December, so there is clear seasonality. In the SA season plot, the lines are flat across the months with no repeating pattern, because the seasonal component has been removed. The only big movement in the SA plot comes from one-time shocks like the 2020 COVID shutdown, which seasonal adjustment does not remove.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in Log of Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    y = "Log(billions of cubic meters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1c.** Production is lowest in the summer months (June through September), rises from October onward, and peaks in the winter months of December and January. This matches intuition: natural gas is heavily used for heating, so demand in Canada is highest in the cold winter months and lowest in the summer. The small dip in February is likely because February has fewer days. The seasonal swings are also smaller in the most recent years, consistent with what we saw in 3.1.

### 4.2 Subseries plot

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )
```

### 4.3 X-13ARIMA-SEATS

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

**4.3a.** December has the highest seasonal factor, at about 1.2 in the 1990s, meaning December sales are roughly 20% above trend. Sales then dip in January and February, to about 10-13% below trend. The seasonal swings appear to shrink over time: the December peak falls from about 1.2 in the 1990s to about 1.15 in recent years, so the holiday spike is a smaller share of sales than it used to be.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.3b.** My X-13 seasonal adjustment matches the official RSAFS series closely: the percent difference is mostly between about -0.5% and +0.5%. The two differ most after the start of COVID, especially around 2021-2023, with differences up to about 1.7%. This is likely because the Census Bureau uses custom settings (for example, special treatment of COVID outliers, holiday, and trading-day effects), while my version uses X-13's default settings, which have the hardest time when the normal seasonal pattern is disrupted.

### 4.4 Linear trend + seasonal dummies

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**4.4a.** The estimated average monthly growth rate of gas production is about 0.4% per month (trend coefficient of 0.004 x 100), or roughly 4.8% per year. June (`season()year6`) has the most significant seasonal effect, with a t-statistic of -4.777: June production is about 0.25 log points (roughly 22%) below January, consistent with lower demand for natural gas in the summer.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.4b.** The fitted line tracks the actual series well from about the mid-1980s to the late 1990s, but it visibly misses in several places: it is far above the actual data in the early 1960s, below it during the 1970s and early 1980s, and above it again after 2000 as actual production levels off. The straight-line trend can't capture the bends in the series' growth.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**4.4c.** The residuals do not look like white noise. The residual plot shows long, slow waves rather than random noise around zero: the residuals are very negative in the early 1960s, positive through the 1970s, near zero in the 1980s-90s, and negative again after 2000. The ACF shows very large autocorrelation (about 0.97 at lag 1) that decays slowly and stays far outside the significance bands at every lag, which indicates leftover trend that the straight-line trend did not capture. The Ljung-Box test confirms this: a statistic of 7,774 with a p-value of about 0, so we reject the null that the residuals are white noise. This suggests a more flexible model is needed to capture the remaining structure in the series.

## Forecast Evaluation

### 5.1 Expanding-window TS-CV

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**5.1a.** The first forecast evaluated is for January 1980 (the first training sample is the 240 months from January 1960 to December 1979), and the last is for February 2005, the last month of data. SNAIVE forecasts much more accurately than the trend + seasonal dummies model: MAE of 0.562 vs. 4.01 and RMSE of 0.702 vs. 4.36 (billions of cubic meters). The two metrics agree, both ranking SNAIVE as more accurate.

### 5.2 Diebold-Mariano test

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

**5.2a.** The DM statistic is -31.278 with a p-value of less thabn 2.2e-16 Since the p-value is below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of equal forecast accuracy: the seasonal random walk's forecasts are statistically significantly more accurate than those of the trend + seasonal dummies model.

### 5.3 Rolling-window TS-CV

```{r}
gas_cv_roll <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_roll |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**5.3a.** With a rolling window, SNAIVE's accuracy is unchanged (MAE 0.562, RMSE 0.702), while TSLM improves a lot (MAE falls from 4.01 to 2.09 and RMSE from 4.36 to 2.42), so TSLM's accuracy changed more. SNAIVE only uses the value from 12 months earlier, so the length of the training sample does not matter. TSLM fits a single straight-line trend, and in 4.4b that line was pulled too steep by the fast 1960s growth. A rolling window drops those early years, so the trend reflects more recent, slower growth and the forecasts overshoot less, though TSLM is still far less accurate than SNAIVE.

## Reflection

The residuals from the linear trend plus seasonal dummies model were far from white noise: they moved in long, slow waves and had autocorrelation close to 1 that died out very slowly. That tells me the model was missing a trend that changes over time, since one straight line could not follow a series that grew quickly, leveled off, grew again, and then flattened. The forecast evaluation pointed the same way: SNAIVE, which simply carries forward the most recent comparable value, beat the trend model badly, and the trend model only improved when a rolling window let it forget the early years. A better model would let the level and trend adapt to recent data instead of fixing them over the whole sample, and would use the strong persistence in the series, so that this month's value helps predict next month's. I expect that means models like ARIMA or exponential smoothing (ETS), which build forecasts from recent observations while still capturing the seasonal pattern.

```{r}
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1c.** The case for logging is stronger than it was for `can_gas`. In levels, the seasonal swings in retail sales grow as sales grow, and after taking logs the swings at the start of the sample are roughly the same size as at the end, which means the swings grew in proportion to the level of the series. This wasn't true for `can_gas`, where the swings grew and then shrank. The log trend is also close to a straight line, consistent with roughly steady percentage growth.

### 3.2 Growth rates

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct  = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth in Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    subtitle = "Month-over-month percent change (direct)",
    x = NULL, y = "Percent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff))

can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Gap Between Direct and Log-Difference Growth Rates",
    subtitle = "Canadian natural gas production",
    x = NULL, y = "Absolute difference (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.2b.** The log difference is a good approximation in most months, with gaps mostly under 0.5 percentage points, but it becomes less accurate in months with very large growth rates, especially in the early 1960s, when the gap reaches about 3 percentage points.

### 3.3 SA vs. NSA growth rates

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.3.** The SA series' month-over-month growth rates hover around 0 percent, apart from large moves during the 2020 COVID shutdown and rebound. The NSA series is much noisier, with growth rates swinging from about -30 to almost 30 percent. This is because the NSA series is not seasonally adjusted: those swings come from its seasonal component. This connects back to 2.7b, where the NSA level spiked every December and dropped every January; in growth rates, that pattern shows up as a large positive growth rate in December and a large negative one in January every year. The SA series has had the seasonal component removed, so its growth rates are much smoother and more stable.

## Seasonality

### 4.1 Season plots

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1b.** In the NSA season plot, every year's line traces the same shape: sales are low in January and February and spike in December, so there is clear seasonality. In the SA season plot, the lines are flat across the months with no repeating pattern, because the seasonal component has been removed. The only big movement in the SA plot comes from one-time shocks like the 2020 COVID shutdown, which seasonal adjustment does not remove.

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in Log of Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    y = "Log(billions of cubic meters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.1c.** Production is lowest in the summer months (June through September), rises from October onward, and peaks in the winter months of December and January. This matches intuition: natural gas is heavily used for heating, so demand in Canada is highest in the cold winter months and lowest in the summer. The small dip in February is likely because February has fewer days. The seasonal swings are also smaller in the most recent years, consistent with what we saw in 3.1.

### 4.2 Subseries plot

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )
```

### 4.3 X-13ARIMA-SEATS

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

**4.3a.** December has the highest seasonal factor, at about 1.2 in the 1990s, meaning December sales are roughly 20% above trend. Sales then dip in January and February, to about 10-13% below trend. The seasonal swings appear to shrink over time: the December peak falls from about 1.2 in the 1990s to about 1.15 in recent years, so the holiday spike is a smaller share of sales than it used to be.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.3b.** My X-13 seasonal adjustment matches the official RSAFS series closely: the percent difference is mostly between about -0.5% and +0.5%. The two differ most after the start of COVID, especially around 2021-2023, with differences up to about 1.7%. This is likely because the Census Bureau uses custom settings (for example, special treatment of COVID outliers, holiday, and trading-day effects), while my version uses X-13's default settings, which have the hardest time when the normal seasonal pattern is disrupted.

### 4.4 Linear trend + seasonal dummies

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**4.4a.** The estimated average monthly growth rate of gas production is about 0.4% per month (trend coefficient of 0.004 x 100), or roughly 4.8% per year. June (`season()year6`) has the most significant seasonal effect, with a t-statistic of -4.777: June production is about 0.25 log points (roughly 22%) below January, consistent with lower demand for natural gas in the summer.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**4.4b.** The fitted line tracks the actual series well from about the mid-1980s to the late 1990s, but it visibly misses in several places: it is far above the actual data in the early 1960s, below it during the 1970s and early 1980s, and above it again after 2000 as actual production levels off. The straight-line trend can't capture the bends in the series' growth.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**4.4c.** The residuals do not look like white noise. The residual plot shows long, slow waves rather than random noise around zero: the residuals are very negative in the early 1960s, positive through the 1970s, near zero in the 1980s-90s, and negative again after 2000. The ACF shows very large autocorrelation (about 0.97 at lag 1) that decays slowly and stays far outside the significance bands at every lag, which indicates leftover trend that the straight-line trend did not capture. The Ljung-Box test confirms this: a statistic of 7,774 with a p-value of about 0, so we reject the null that the residuals are white noise. This suggests a more flexible model is needed to capture the remaining structure in the series.

## Forecast Evaluation

### 5.1 Expanding-window TS-CV

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**5.1a.** The first forecast evaluated is for January 1980 (the first training sample is the 240 months from January 1960 to December 1979), and the last is for February 2005, the last month of data. SNAIVE forecasts much more accurately than the trend + seasonal dummies model: MAE of 0.562 vs. 4.01 and RMSE of 0.702 vs. 4.36 (billions of cubic meters). The two metrics agree, both ranking SNAIVE as more accurate.

### 5.2 Diebold-Mariano test

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

**5.2a.** \[FILL IN from the output above: The DM statistic is \_\_\_ with a p-value of \_\_\_.\] Since the p-value is below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis of equal forecast accuracy: the seasonal random walk's forecasts are statistically significantly more accurate than those of the trend + seasonal dummies model.

### 5.3 Rolling-window TS-CV

```{r}
gas_cv_roll <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_roll |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  select(.model, MAE, RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**5.3a.** With a rolling window, SNAIVE's accuracy is unchanged (MAE 0.562, RMSE 0.702), while TSLM improves a lot (MAE falls from 4.01 to 2.09 and RMSE from 4.36 to 2.42), so TSLM's accuracy changed more. SNAIVE only uses the value from 12 months earlier, so the length of the training sample does not matter. TSLM fits a single straight-line trend, and in 4.4b that line was pulled too steep by the fast 1960s growth. A rolling window drops those early years, so the trend reflects more recent, slower growth and the forecasts overshoot less, though TSLM is still far less accurate than SNAIVE.

## Reflection

The residuals from the linear trend plus seasonal dummies model were far from white noise, they moved in long, slow waves and had autocorrelation close to 1 that died out very slowly. That tells me the model was missing a trend that changes over time, since one straight line could not follow a series that grew quickly, leveled off, grew again, and then flattened. The forecast evaluation told us the same thing, SNAIVE, which simply carries forward the most recent comparable value, beat the trend model badly, and the trend model only improved when a rolling window let it forget the early years. A better model would let the level and trend adapt to recent data instead of fixing them over the whole sample, and would use the strong persistence in the series, so that this month's value helps predict next month's. I expect that means models like ARIMA or exponential smoothing (ETS), which build forecasts from recent observations while still capturing the seasonal pattern.
